questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Inequality When the Base of the Exponential is Between Zero and One
questions.worked_solution:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x+4}-3 & \le 1 \\ {(\frac{1}{3})}^{x+4} & \le 4.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡[{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x+4}] & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡4 \\ (x+4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3}) & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡4 \\ (x+4)(\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡3) & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡4 \\ -(x+4)\operatorname{ln}⁡3 & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡4\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, note that $-\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ is a negative quantity, so when we divide both sides by it, we need to flip the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+4 & \ge -\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\ x & \ge -\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}-4\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Inequality with Exponential Functions on Both Sides
questions.worked_solution:
Since ${12}^{x}$ is always positive and $-{2}^{6x-1}$ is always negative, we always have

$$
-{2}^{6x-1}<{12}^{x}.
$$

This means that the given inequality is satisfied by all real values of $x.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Inequality When the Exponential is Compared to Zero or a Negative Number
questions.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the exponential term:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2x+7}+1 & <-5 \\ 2{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2x+7} & <-6 \\ {(\frac{1}{3})}^{2x+7} & <-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall that a positive number raised to any real power is always positive. Since $\frac{1}{3}>0,$ we have

$$
{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2x+7}>0
$$

for every real value of $x.$

Therefore, ${(\frac{1}{3})}^{2x+7}$ cannot be less than $-3.$ Hence, the inequality

$$
{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2x+7}<-3
$$

has no solutions.

questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Inequality with Exponential Functions on Both Sides
questions.worked_solution:
Since $(0.98)^{3x-1}$ is always positive and $-(0.75)^{2-3x}$ is always negative, we always have

$$
-(0.75)^{2-3x}<(0.98)^{3x-1}.
$$

This means that the given inequality is satisfied by all real values of $x.$

Therefore,

$$
-\infty <x<\infty 
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Inequality When the Base of the Exponential is Between Zero and One
questions.worked_solution:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}{(\frac{3}{5})}^{x} & \le 3\sqrt{3} \\ {(\frac{3}{5})}^{x} & \le 3\cdot 3\sqrt{3} \\ {(\frac{3}{5})}^{x} & \le 9\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡[{(\frac{3}{5})}^{x}] & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡(9\sqrt{3}) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{5}) & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡(9\sqrt{3}) \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡5) & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡(9\sqrt{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, note that $\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡5$ is a negative quantity, so when we divide both sides by it, we need to flip the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & \ge \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(9\sqrt{3})}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\end{aligned}
$$
